newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strauss-Kahn named French finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Strauss-Kahn named French finance minister.

text.p: Dominique Strauss-Kahn, architect of the French Socialist party's economic policy, was named on Wednesday to the key post of finance minister in Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government.

Strauss-Kahn, 48, a former industry minister, made his name as a strong advocate of the French concept of a mixed economy coupling gradual free-market reform with the defence of a strong state role in industry.

A close confidant of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, he has championed the party line on Europe which favours closer integration and monetary union but demands further talks on the details of a planned euro currency in 1999.

He was among the first to suggest criteria in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union be interpreted politically rather than in strict mathematical terms, including the requirement to cut public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
"Even if it's clear that public deficits cannot be allowed to slip, there is no point in making an unjustified dogma out of three percent," he said last month.
He has also advocated a slightly "softer" euro, saying it should be used to boost job creation and economic growth.
"If the Euro is to serve a purpose, it should not be overvalued against the dollar on the one hand and it should also contribute to stimulating the economy and unemployment," he said in early May.

Industry and trade minister in the short-lived 1991-92 government of prime minister Edith Cresson, Strauss-Kahn won the respect of the corporate sector for his role as a counterweight to what industrialists saw as Cresson's policy excesses.

With the same portfolio in the 1992-93 Socialist government of Pierre Beregovoy, Strauss-Kahn distinguished himself as a vocal defender of French interests in negotiations over the GATT international free trade agreement.

In an illustration of his commitment to a strong government role in industry, he used his opposition seat in parliament to strongly oppose the privatisation programme enacted by Jacques Chirac, now president, when he was prime minister in 1986-88.

Ousted from his National Assembly seat when the Socialists were routed in the last election in 1993, Strauss-Kahn's re-entry into the corridors of power completes a journey emblematic of the left's own recent history.
Married to star television journalist Anne Sinclair, Strauss-Kahn chaired the National Assembly finance committee before joining Cresson's government in May 1991.
Dominique Gaston Andre Strauss-Kahn was born on April 25, 1949 at Neuilly sur Seine, a western Paris suburb.

He followed in the footsteps of his father and obtained a law degree, but also studied at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales elite business school and has advanced degrees in political science, statistics and economics.
He entered parliament in 1986, when as a senior Socialist Party official he was elected for the Alpine Haute Savoie department. He was re-elected in 1988 for Val d'Oise near Paris.
